source_text: Meretur autem et ab honestis exsecrationem, et ab illa iustitia, cuius hic tota causa vertitur, legitimam condemnationem. Omnibus itaque aulaeis reductis profer aliquando luce palam, per quid doceas naturale esse peccatum. Certe nihil superius falso vel de divinae laude iustitiae, vel de culpae definitione collectum est. Ostende ergo, haec duo in parvulis posse constare: si nullum est sine voluntate peccatum, si nulla voluntas, ubi non est explicata libertas, si non est libertas, ubi non est facultas per rationem electionis; quo monstro peccatum in infantibus invenitur, qui rationis usum non habent? Igitur nec eligendi facultatem, ac per hoc nec voluntatem; atque his irrefutabiliter concessis, nec aliquod omnino peccatum. His igitur molibus pressus, videamus quo eruperis. Nullo, inquis, peccato parvuli premuntur suo, sed premuntur alieno [n56] . Necdum claruit quid mali sentias. Suspicamur enim te ad invidiam cuiuspiam hominis, cuius iniquitatem ut Poenus orator exprimeres, haec in medium protulisse. Apud quem igitur impollutam innocentiam scelus gravavit externum? Quis ille fuit, qui hos adiudicaret reos, tam excors, tam trux, tam oblitus Dei et aequitatis, barbarus perduellis? Laudamus prorsus ingenium tuum; apparet eruditio, non potuisti aliter, dignam generis humani odio, iudicis nescio cuius, immo tyranni allegare personam, quam iurando non solum eum non pepercisse his qui nihil peccavissent, verum etiam his qui nec peccare potuissent. Solet quippe apud suspiciosum animum bona conscientia laborare pro defensione sui, ne forte deliquerit, quia delinquere vel potuit; absolute autem vindicatur a crimine, qui ipsa rei impossibilitate defenditur. Pande igitur quis est iste innocentium addictor. Respondens: Deus; percussisti quidem animum, sed quoniam vix tantum sacrilegium fidem meretur, quid dixeris ambigamus. Scimus enim homonyme usurpari nomen hoc posse: Sunt quippe dii multi et domini multi; nobis tamen unus est Deus Pater ex quo omnia, et unus est Dominus Iesus Christus per quem omnia [n57] . Quem igitur Deum in crimen vocas? Hic tu, sacerdos religiosissime, rhetorque doctissime, exhalas tristius et horridius aliquid, quam vel Amsancti vallis, vel puteus Averni, immo scelestius quam ipsa in his locis idolorum cultura commiserat [n58] . Deus, ais, ipse qui commendat suam caritatem in nobis [n59] , qui dilexit nos, et Filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis illum tradidit [n60] , ipse sic iudicat, ipse est nascentium persecutor, ipse pro mala voluntate aeternis ignibus parvulos tradit, quos nec bonam, nec malam voluntatem scit habere potuisse. Post hanc ergo sententiam, tam immanem, tam sacrilegam, tam funestam, si sanis iudicibus uteremur, nihil praeter exsecrationem tui referre deberem. Iusta enim, et probabili gravitate, indignum te disputatione censerem, qui eo usque a religione, ab eruditione, a communibus postremo sensibus aufugisses ut, quod vix ulla barbaries, Dominum tuum criminosum putares.
pass_a_gloss: But it deserves both execration from the honorable, and from that justice, whose whole cause is here being turned, a lawful condemnation. With all tapestries therefore drawn back, bring forth at last openly in the light, through what you teach sin to be natural. Certainly nothing gathered above either from praise of divine justice or from the definition of guilt is false. Show therefore that these two can stand in little ones: if there is no sin without will, if no will where freedom has not been unfolded, if there is not freedom where there is not a faculty through reason of choice; by what monster is sin found in infants, who do not have the use of reason? Therefore neither the faculty of choosing, and through this neither will; and these things having been granted irrefutably, neither any sin at all. Pressed therefore by these masses, let us see where you have burst out. By no sin, you say, are little ones pressed of their own, but they are pressed by another's. Not yet has it become clear what evil you sense. For we suspect that you, to work ill-will against some human whose iniquity you as a Punic orator would express, have brought these things into the midst. Before whom therefore did an outside crime weigh down unpolluted innocence? Who was that one who would adjudge these guilty, so mindless, so savage, so forgetful of God and of equity, a barbarian enemy? We praise outright your talent; learning appears, you could not otherwise allege a person of some judge, nay of a tyrant, worthy of the hatred of the human race, than by swearing that he not only did not spare those who had sinned nothing, but even those who could not even have sinned. For before a suspicious mind a good conscience is accustomed to labor for defense of itself, lest perhaps it have offended, because it at least could offend; but he is absolutely vindicated from the crime who is defended by the very impossibility of the thing. Open therefore who this condemner of innocents is. Answering: God; you have indeed struck the mind, but since so great a sacrilege scarcely earns belief, let us be in doubt what you have said. For we know that this name can be used homonymously: There are indeed many gods and many lords; for us nevertheless there is one God the Father from whom all things, and one is the Lord Jesus Christ through whom all things. Which God therefore do you call into the charge? Here you, most religious priest and most learned rhetor, exhale something sadder and more horrible than either the valley of Amsanctus or the pit of Avernus, nay more criminal than the very cult of idols had committed in these places. God, you say, himself who commends his love in us, who loved us, and did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us, himself so judges, himself is the persecutor of those being born, himself for an evil will hands little ones over to eternal fires, whom he knows could have had neither a good nor an evil will. After this sentence therefore, so monstrous, so sacrilegious, so deadly, if we were using sane judges, I ought to bring back nothing besides execration of you. For with just and probable gravity I would judge you unworthy of disputation, who had fled to that point from religion, from learning, finally from common senses that, what scarcely any barbarism, you would think your Lord criminal.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS libertas; Blaise moral freedom to will or refuse

pass_b_english: Sin deserves both the abhorrence of honorable people and lawful condemnation from the justice that is the whole subject of our present inquiry. With all the curtains drawn back, bring into the open at last the grounds on which you teach that sin is inherent in nature. Surely nothing we established above, either in praise of divine justice or in defining guilt, was false. Show, then, that these two things can hold together in infants. If there is no sin without will, no will where freedom has not developed, and no freedom where there is no ability to choose through reason, by what monstrosity is sin found in infants, who have no use of reason? They therefore have no capacity for choice and consequently no will; and once these undeniable points are granted, they have no sin whatsoever. Pressed by these massive arguments, let us see where you break out. You say: “Infants are weighed down by no sin of their own, but by another's” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 1.22).

The evil of your view is not yet clear. We suspect that you have introduced this point to arouse hostility toward some man whose injustice you wish to portray with your African rhetoric. In whose court, then, did someone else's crime burden unstained innocence? Who was that barbarous enemy, so mindless, so savage, so forgetful of God and fairness, who sentenced these infants as guilty? We certainly praise your talent; your education shows! You could not otherwise have depicted some judge, or rather tyrant, as deserving the hatred of the human race than by swearing that he spared not only no one who had committed no sin, but not even those who could not have sinned. Before a suspicious mind, a good conscience commonly labors in its own defense against the possibility that it did wrong, since it at least could have done wrong. But someone defended by the very impossibility of the act is completely cleared of the charge.

Reveal, then, who this condemner of innocents is. You answer: “God.” You have indeed struck my mind a blow. But since so great a sacrilege scarcely deserves belief, let us hesitate over what you have said. We know that this name can be applied to different beings: “There are many gods and many lords; for us, however, there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:5–6). Which God, then, are you charging with a crime? Here you, most religious priest and most learned rhetorician, breathe out something more dreadful and horrible than the valley of Amsanctus or the pit of Avernus, indeed something more criminal than the worship of idols committed in those places (compare Virgil, Aeneid 7.565).

You say: “God himself, who commends his love toward us (Romans 5:8), who loved us and did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us (Romans 8:32), judges in this way. He himself is the persecutor of newborn children. He hands infants over to eternal fires for an evil will, although he knows they could have had neither a good nor an evil will.” After this statement, so monstrous, so sacrilegious, so deadly, if we had sane judges I ought to answer with nothing but abhorrence of you. With just and commendable seriousness I would judge you unworthy of discussion. You have fled so far from religion, from education, and finally from ordinary human understanding that you consider your Lord a criminal, something scarcely any barbarian would do.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
